lessons.title: Milk Composition and Quality Parameters
lessons.body: Milk is about 87% water, 3.5% fat, 3.4% protein, 4.8% lactose, and 0.7% minerals. For ice cream, you need to know these numbers because they affect texture and sweetness. In Africa, fresh cow milk is common, but you can also use camel, goat, or sheep milk. Each has different fat and protein levels. For example, goat milk has smaller fat globules, which can make ice cream creamier but also more prone to goaty flavor. Always test milk quality before use. A simple way is to check smell and appearance: fresh milk should smell clean, not sour, and look white to creamy. Use a lactometer to check density; it should read between 1.026 and 1.032 at 20Â°C. If it's lower, the milk may be watered down. Also, do a clot-on-boiling test: boil a small sample; if it curdles, the milk is acidic and will ruin your ice cream. For ice cream, you want milk with low bacteria count. If you don't have a lab, pasteurize milk at 72Â°C for 15 seconds, then cool quickly. In many African settings, milk is often unpasteurized, so this step is critical. Also, consider using milk powder if fresh milk is scarce. But fresh milk gives better flavor. Remember, milk quality directly affects the final product: high-fat milk makes richer ice cream, while high-protein milk can make it too icy if not balanced. So, measure your ingredients carefully. Use a thermometer and a lactometer; these are cheap tools available in agricultural supply shops. Always source from healthy animals and keep milk cold (below 4Â°C) until use. If you're buying from a local farmer, ask about animal health and feed. Good milk is the foundation of good ice cream.

lessons.title: Cream: Types, Fat Content, and Sourcing
lessons.body: Cream is the fat-rich part of milk that rises to the top when milk is left to stand. In ice cream, cream gives richness, smoothness, and helps trap air. The fat content of cream varies: light cream has 18-30% fat, whipping cream has 30-36%, and heavy cream has 36-40%. In Africa, you can buy cream from dairy processors or make your own by skimming the top of settled milk. To make cream at home, let fresh milk sit in a cool place for 12-24 hours, then skim the top layer with a ladle. This gives you a cream with about 20-30% fat, depending on the milk. For consistent results, you can also use a cream separator, but these are expensive. Instead, many small-scale producers use a simple method: heat milk to 40Â°C, then let it cool and skim. The fat content affects your ice cream's texture: more fat means creamier, but too much can make it heavy and coat your mouth. A typical ice cream mix has 10-16% fat. So, if you use heavy cream (36% fat), you'll need less than if you use light cream. When sourcing cream, check for freshness: it should smell sweet, not sour. If you're buying from a market, ask for unpasteurized cream and pasteurize it yourself at 72Â°C for 15 seconds. In hot African climates, cream spoils quickly, so keep it refrigerated. If you can't get fresh cream, you can use butter or ghee, but these change the flavor. For a local twist, try using cream from zebu cattle, which has higher fat content. Always measure fat content using a butyrometer if available, or use the formula: fat% = (cream volume / milk volume) x 100. This helps you adjust recipes. Remember, cream is expensive, so use it wisely. You can also blend cream with milk to get the right fat level. For example, to make 1 liter of 12% fat mix, mix 333 ml of 36% cream with 667 ml of skim milk. This saves money and gives consistent results.

lessons.title: Concentrated Milks: Evaporated, Condensed, and Powdered
lessons.body: Concentrated milks are milk with some water removed. They are useful in Africa because they last longer without refrigeration and are easy to transport. Evaporated milk is unsweetened and has about 7.5% fat and 25% milk solids. Condensed milk is sweetened with sugar (about 40-45% sugar) and has 8% fat. Powdered milk is dried milk with less than 5% moisture; it can be whole (26% fat) or skim (1% fat). In ice cream, these ingredients add milk solids, fat, and flavor. They also help control ice crystal formation because they bind water. For example, using 100g of skim milk powder in a 1-liter mix can improve texture and reduce iciness. But you must rehydrate them properly: for powdered milk, mix with warm water (40Â°C) at a ratio of 1 part powder to 4 parts water for whole milk, or 1:8 for skim. Let it sit for 20 minutes to fully dissolve. Evaporated milk can be used straight from the can, but if you want to substitute for fresh milk, mix equal parts evaporated milk and water. Condensed milk is already sweet, so reduce the sugar in your recipe. For instance, if a recipe calls for 200g sugar and you use 300g condensed milk (which contains about 120g sugar), add only 80g extra sugar. In Africa, these products are often imported, so check expiry dates and seals. If you open a can, use it within 3 days and refrigerate. Powdered milk is the most shelf-stable; keep it dry and cool. For best results, use a blender to mix powders into your liquid to avoid lumps. Also, note that concentrated milks can have a cooked flavor, especially evaporated milk. To minimize this, choose brands with no additives. You can also make your own evaporated milk by simmering fresh milk down to half its volume, but this takes time and fuel. For small-scale ice cream makers, powdered milk is often the most cost-effective. It allows you to adjust fat and solids easily. For example, to increase milk solids without adding fat, use skim milk powder. To add fat, use whole milk powder or cream. Always calculate your mix to balance fat, sugar, and solids. A simple formula: total solids should be 36-40% of the mix. This includes fat, protein, lactose, and added sugar. Concentrated milks help you hit that target.

lessons.title: Whey and Dairy By-Products in Ice Cream
lessons.body: Whey is the liquid left after cheese-making. It contains about 0.8% protein, 5% lactose, and little fat. In Africa, whey is often discarded, but it can be used in ice cream to reduce cost and add solids. However, whey has a high lactose content, which can cause sandiness (lactose crystals) if too much is used. A safe limit is 2-3% whey powder in the mix. Whey protein concentrate (WPC) is a better option: it has 35-80% protein and improves texture by binding water and stabilizing air bubbles. You can buy WPC from dairy suppliers or use it as a by-product from local cheese makers. Other by-products include buttermilk (from butter-making) and skim milk. Buttermilk adds a tangy flavor and helps emulsify fat. In ice cream, using 5-10% buttermilk can enhance creaminess. Skim milk is essentially milk without fat; it adds protein and lactose but no fat. When using by-products, always pasteurize them first. For whey, heat to 72Â°C for 15 seconds, then cool. If you're using whey from a local cheese maker, ask if it's been pasteurized; if not, do it yourself. Also, whey can have a salty taste if from salted cheese, so taste before adding. In terms of cost, whey is often free or cheap, making it attractive for small businesses. But don't overuse it: too much whey can make ice cream icy and weak-flavored. A typical recipe might use 10% whey powder, 5% buttermilk powder, and the rest from milk and cream. You can also use whey to replace some of the water in your mix. For example, if a recipe calls for 1 liter of milk, use 800 ml milk and 200 ml whey. This reduces cost and adds nutrients. However, whey has a high mineral content, which can affect flavor. So, start with small amounts and adjust. In Africa, whey is also used in animal feed, but with proper handling, it can be a valuable ice cream ingredient. Always store whey refrigerated and use within 2 days. If you can't get fresh whey, whey powder is a good alternative. It has a long shelf life and is easy to measure. Use 1 part whey powder to 9 parts water to reconstitute. Then treat it like fresh whey. Remember, by-products are not waste; they are resources. With creativity, you can make delicious ice cream while saving money.

lessons.title: Butterfat Alternatives and Their Impact on Texture
lessons.body: Butterfat is the gold standard for ice cream, but it's expensive and not always available in Africa. Alternatives include vegetable oils (coconut, palm, sunflower), butter, ghee, and emulsifiers. Each affects texture differently. Coconut oil is solid at room temperature in cooler climates but melts quickly in the mouth, giving a cool sensation. It has a distinct flavor, so use refined coconut oil if you want neutral taste. Palm oil is semi-solid and cheap, but it can leave a waxy mouthfeel. Sunflower oil is liquid and makes ice cream softer; it's best used in small amounts (2-5% of mix). Butter and ghee are dairy fats, so they give a rich flavor, but they contain water and milk solids that can affect freezing. Ghee is clarified butter, so it's pure fat and has a high smoke point; it's great for ice cream but expensive. When replacing butterfat, you need to consider the fat's melting point. Butterfat melts at about 32Â°C, close to body temperature, which gives a clean melt. Coconut oil melts at 24Â°C, so it feels cool. Palm oil melts at 35Â°C, so it can feel waxy. To mimic butterfat, you can blend oils. For example, mix 70% coconut oil and 30% sunflower oil to get a melting point around 28Â°C. Also, you may need emulsifiers like lecithin (from soy or sunflower) to stabilize the mix. Use 0.2-0.5% lecithin by weight. Without emulsifiers, oil can separate and create greasy ice cream. Another alternative is to use eggs (yolks) as natural emulsifiers; 2-3 yolks per liter of mix can replace some fat and add richness. But eggs add a custard flavor. In Africa, shea butter is a local fat that is solid at room temperature and melts at 35Â°C. It can be used but has a strong smell; refine it first. When using alternatives, adjust your recipe: replace 1 kg butterfat with 0.8 kg oil plus 0.2 kg emulsifier. Also, reduce water if using butter or ghee, as they contain some water. Test small batches to see how the texture changes. The goal is to achieve a smooth, creamy ice cream that melts nicely. Too much solid fat makes it greasy; too much liquid oil makes it soupy. So, balance is key. Always label your product if you use non-dairy fats, as some customers may have allergies or preferences.

lessons.title: Evaluating Dairy Ingredient Quality for Ice Cream
lessons.body: Before you make ice cream, you must evaluate your dairy ingredients. Poor quality means poor ice cream. Start with smell: fresh milk and cream should smell sweet and clean. If it smells sour, yeasty, or like a barn, don't use it. Next, look at color: milk should be white to creamy, cream should be yellowish-white. Any blue, pink, or brown spots indicate spoilage or contamination. Then, check texture: milk should be smooth, not lumpy or watery. For cream, it should be thick but pourable. If it's clumpy, it may be starting to turn to butter. For powders, check for lumps and caking; they should be free-flowing. If they're hard, they've absorbed moisture and may have bacteria. Always check expiry dates. For fresh milk, do a simple acidity test: mix 10 ml milk with 5 drops of phenolphthalein and titrate with 0.1N sodium hydroxide until pink. The volume used should be 1.4-1.8 ml for fresh milk. If higher, it's acidic. A cheaper test: boil a spoonful; if it curdles, it's too acidic. For fat content, use a butyrometer or the Gerber method. For protein, you can use a formaldehyde titration, but that's advanced. Instead, rely on taste: milk with high protein tastes slightly sweet and coats the tongue. For powders, reconstitute a sample and taste it. It should taste like fresh milk, not cardboard or burnt. Also, test solubility: mix 10g powder in 100ml warm water; it should dissolve within 1 minute with stirring. If it leaves lumps, it's low quality. For whey and by-products, check for off-flavors and saltiness. If using whey from cheese, taste it; if it's too salty, rinse it with water or use less. For butterfat alternatives, check for rancidity: smell and taste a small amount. If it smells like crayons or paint, it's rancid. Also, check the melting point by heating a small sample; it should melt smoothly. In Africa, where refrigeration is limited, always buy from trusted suppliers and keep ingredients cool. Use a thermometer to ensure milk is below 4Â°C. If you're buying from a market, ask for a sample and do a quick smell and taste test. For large batches, consider sending a sample to a lab for bacteria count. But for small-scale, your senses are your best tools. Document your evaluations: note the source, date, and results. This helps you identify reliable suppliers. Remember, good ice cream starts with good ingredients. Don't cut corners on quality.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Dairy Ingredients and Their Functions in Ice Cream

This practical reference module is designed for African ice cream producers, dairy processors, and agribusiness entrepreneurs who need to make fast, cost-effective, and quality-driven decisions about dairy ingredients. Whether you are sourcing milk from smallholder farmers in Kenya, importing cream powder into Nigeria, or formulating with local whey streams in South Africa, this guide gives you the technical benchmarks and business logic to protect your margins and your brand.

Dairy ingredients in ice cream do four jobs: they supply fat for richness and texture, protein for structure and overrun stability, lactose and minerals for flavour and freezing point control, and water for the mix itself. In African markets, where cold chain costs are high and imported dairy inputs can consume 40â60% of ingredient spend, understanding the function of each ingredient is a commercial survival skill.

1. Milk Composition and Quality Parameters

Milk is roughly 87% water, 3.5â5% fat, 3.2â3.5% protein, 4.5â5% lactose, and 0.7% minerals. For ice cream, the critical quality parameters are fat content, protein content, somatic cell count (SCC), total bacterial count (TBC), antibiotic residues, and freezing point. In many African markets, milk is collected from smallholders and delivered warm, so TBC and SCC are the two most common causes of off-flavour, poor overrun, and short shelf life.

Business rule of thumb: if your raw milk TBC exceeds 1,000,000 cfu/ml or SCC exceeds 400,000 cells/ml, do not use it for premium ice cream. Divert it to lower-value products such as yoghurt or animal feed. Pay a premium for chilled, low-SCC milk â it is cheaper than fixing a spoiled batch.

Table 1: Raw Milk Quality Parameters for Ice Cream Production
Parameter Target for Premium Ice Cream Acceptable for Standard Reject / Divert
Total Bacterial Count (cfu/ml)< 100,000100,000 â 500,000> 1,000,000
Somatic Cell Count (cells/ml)< 200,000200,000 â 400,000> 400,000
Milk Fat (%)3.8 â 4.53.2 â 3.8< 3.0
Milk Protein (%)> 3.33.0 â 3.3< 2.9
Antibiotic ResiduesNegativeNegativePositive
Freezing Point (Â°C)-0.54 to -0.52-0.55 to -0.50> -0.50 (added water)

Sources: IDF (2019) Bulletin of the IDF No. 500: Milk Quality; FAO (2011) Milk and Dairy Products in Human Nutrition; Kenya Dairy Board quality standards.

2. Cream: Types, Fat Content, and Sourcing

Cream is the primary fat source in premium ice cream. In Africa, cream is often the most expensive dairy input, especially when imported. Local sourcing options include fresh cream from dairy processors, frozen cream, plastic cream (65â80% fat), and butter. Fat content in the final mix typically ranges from 8â16%, with 10â12% being the commercial sweet spot for cost and creaminess.

Fresh cream (35â40% fat) gives the cleanest flavour but has a 5â7 day refrigerated shelf life. Frozen cream (40â45% fat) is more practical for producers without daily milk supply, but must be thawed carefully to avoid churning. Plastic cream (65â80% fat) is cost-effective for transport but requires high-shear mixing. In East Africa, cream is often sourced from processors such as Brookside, Sameer, or local cooperatives. In West Africa, imported frozen cream and butter are common because local cream supply is thin.

Table 2: Cream and Butterfat Sources â Cost, Function, and Sourcing in Africa
Source Fat Content Function in Ice Cream African Sourcing Note Relative Cost
Fresh cream35 â 40%Clean flavour, best textureEast/Southern Africa dairy processorsHigh
Frozen cream40 â 45%Good texture, longer storageImported or local frozen stockMedium-High
Plastic cream65 â 80%Cost-effective fat, needs mixingImported, limited local supplyMedium
Butter (unsalted)80 â 82%Rich flavour, easy storageLocal or importedMedium
Anhydrous Milk Fat (AMF)99.8%Long shelf life, neutral flavourImported, used in dry mixesHigh
Vegetable fat blends100%Cheapest fat, alters textureLocal palm/ coconut blendsLow

Sources: Goff & Hartel (2013) Ice Cream, 7th ed.; FAO (2011); industry price surveys, East African dairy processors (2023â2024).

3. Concentrated Milks: Evaporated, Condensed, and Powdered

Concentrated milks are the workhorses of African ice cream production because they reduce transport costs, extend shelf life, and allow production without daily fresh milk. Evaporated milk (unsweetened, ~7.5% fat, 25% solids) adds richness and body. Sweetened condensed milk (8% fat, 28% sugar, 45% solids) adds sweetness, body, and controls freezing point â but it counts toward your sugar budget. Skim milk powder (SMP, 34% protein, <1% fat) and whole milk powder (WMP, 26% fat, 25% protein) are the most common imported dairy inputs in Africa.

Key business insight: SMP is usually cheaper per kilogram of protein than liquid milk, but it must be reconstituted correctly (typically 10â12% solids) and given time to hydrate (30â60 minutes) before pasteurisation. Poor hydration causes sandy texture and low overrun. In Nigeria, Ghana, and Kenya, SMP and WMP are often imported from the EU, New Zealand, or India. Always check for heat classification (low, medium, high heat) â high-heat powders are better for ice cream because they improve water binding and reduce icy texture.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Aflatoxin and Antibiotic Residues in Dairy Ingredients:

In many African markets, milk and dairy powders can contain aflatoxin M1 (from contaminated animal feed) or antibiotic residues (from untreated mastitis). Both survive pasteurisation and can enter your ice cream. Aflatoxin M1 is a carcinogen; antibiotic residues can cause allergic reactions and undermine consumer trust. Always demand a certificate of analysis (CoA) for every dairy ingredient batch, test incoming milk with rapid test kits where available, and reject any batch with aflatoxin M1 above 0.5 Âµg/kg or positive antibiotic residues. This is a legal requirement in most African countries and a commercial necessity for export or supermarket supply.

4. Whey and Dairy By-Products in Ice Cream

Whey is the liquid remaining after cheese or casein production. In Africa, cheese production is growing in Kenya, Ethiopia, and South Africa, creating opportunities to use whey as a low-cost dairy solid. Sweet whey powder (11â13% protein, 70â75% lactose) and whey protein concentrate (WPC 35â80% protein) can replace 10â25% of SMP in ice cream mix without major quality loss, provided you adjust for lactose and mineral content.

Whey improves overrun and reduces cost, but too much whey causes sandy texture, weak body, and faster meltdown because of its high lactose and low casein. Practical rule: replace no more than 25% of your milk solids with sweet whey powder, and never use acid whey (from cottage cheese or Greek yoghurt) in premium ice cream â it gives a salty, chalky taste. For African producers, whey is a strategic cost-reduction tool, especially in markets where SMP is imported and expensive.

5. Butterfat Alternatives and Their Impact on Texture

Butterfat alternatives include vegetable fats (palm, coconut, palm kernel, shea), anhydrous milk fat (AMF), and blended fats. They are used to cut cost, extend shelf life, and improve heat resistance. However, they change texture: vegetable fats can make ice cream feel waxy or greasy, reduce flavour release, and lower meltdown quality. AMF is closer to butterfat but still lacks the full flavour profile of fresh cream.

In Africa, coconut oil and palm oil blends are common because they are locally available and cheaper than butterfat. Shea butter is an emerging option in West Africa, but it has a strong flavour and requires refining. Business guidance: if you use vegetable fat, keep it below 30% of total fat, use high-quality refined blends, and declare it clearly on the label. Premium and export markets will reject ice cream made with non-dairy fat unless it is explicitly labelled as "frozen dessert."

6. Evaluating Dairy Ingredient Quality for Ice Cream

Quality evaluation is a commercial control point. Every batch of dairy ingredient should be checked for appearance, odour, solubility, fat, protein, moisture, and microbiological safety. For powders, check for lumps, off-colours, and burnt or stale smell. For cream, check for separation, sourness, and freeze-thaw damage. For liquid milk, check temperature, acidity, and antibiotic residues.

In practice, African ice cream producers should build a simple ingredient receipt log with batch number, supplier, date, temperature, sensory result, and CoA status. This protects you in disputes, supports traceability, and helps you negotiate better prices with suppliers who consistently meet specification.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Check TBC and SCC before accepting raw milk â reject above 1,000,000 cfu/ml or 400,000 cells/ml.
  • Demand a CoA for every dairy powder, cream, or butter batch, including aflatoxin M1 and antibiotic residue results.
  • Verify fat and protein content â use a lactometer, Gerber test, or rapid analyser; do not rely on supplier claims alone.
  • Hydrate milk powder fully (30â60 minutes) before pasteurisation to avoid sandy texture and low overrun.
  • Limit whey replacement to 25% of milk solids; never use acid whey in premium ice cream.
  • Keep vegetable fat below 30% of total fat and label accurately to avoid regulatory and consumer backlash.
  • Store powders cool and dry (<25Â°C, <65% RH) and use within 6â12 months; cream must stay at 0â4Â°C.
  • Log every batch â supplier, date, temperature, sensory result, and CoA status â for traceability and negotiation.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Dairy Production and Products (free technical resources on milk quality and processing).
  • FAO (2011) â Milk and Dairy Products in Human Nutrition (free PDF, global reference).
  • International Dairy Federation (IDF) â standards and bulletins on milk quality and dairy ingredients.
  • Codex Alimentarius â international standards for milk and milk products, including ice cream.
  • International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) â African dairy value chain research and practical guides.

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course "Ice Cream Production." For training, mentorship, or business advisory, contact your local Rise AFRICA hub.

quiz.q: What is the approximate water content of milk?
quiz.explanation: Milk is about 87% water, which is the largest component.

quiz.q: Which test can indicate if milk is acidic and will curdle when boiled?
quiz.explanation: The clot-on-boiling test shows if milk is acidic by curdling when heated.

quiz.q: What is the fat content range for whipping cream?
quiz.explanation: Whipping cream typically contains 30-36% fat, ideal for whipping.

quiz.q: How can you make cream at home without a separator?
options: B) Let milk sit and skim the top
quiz.explanation: Letting fresh milk sit allows cream to rise, which can be skimmed off.

quiz.q: What is the typical fat content of heavy cream?
quiz.explanation: Heavy cream has 36-40% fat, making it very rich.

quiz.q: Which of these is a concentrated milk?
quiz.explanation: Evaporated milk is milk with water removed, making it concentrated.

quiz.q: What is the sugar content of condensed milk?
quiz.explanation: Condensed milk is sweetened and contains about 40-45% sugar.

quiz.q: How should you reconstitute skim milk powder for use in ice cream?
options: A) 1 part powder to 2 parts water
B) 1 part powder to 4 parts water
C) 1 part powder to 8 parts water
D) 1 part powder to 10 parts water
quiz.explanation: Skim milk powder is typically reconstituted at 1:8 ratio for skim milk.

quiz.q: What is a safe limit for whey powder in an ice cream mix to avoid sandiness?
quiz.explanation: Using more than 2-3% whey powder can cause lactose crystals and sandiness.

quiz.q: Which dairy by-product is known for its tangy flavor and emulsifying properties?
quiz.explanation: Buttermilk adds tang and helps emulsify fat in ice cream.

quiz.q: What is the main protein in whey?
quiz.explanation: Whey contains lactalbumin and lactoglobulin as its main proteins.

quiz.q: Why should you pasteurize whey before using it in ice cream?
quiz.explanation: Pasteurization kills pathogens that may be present in raw whey.

quiz.q: Which oil is solid at room temperature and melts at about 24Â°C, giving a cool sensation?
quiz.explanation: Coconut oil melts at 24Â°C, providing a cool mouthfeel.

quiz.q: What is the melting point of butterfat?
quiz.explanation: Butterfat melts at about 32Â°C, close to body temperature.

quiz.q: Which emulsifier is commonly used to stabilize oil in ice cream?
quiz.explanation: Lecithin, from soy or sunflower, is a natural emulsifier.

quiz.q: How much lecithin is typically used in an ice cream mix?
quiz.explanation: Lecithin is used at 0.2-0.5% by weight to stabilize emulsions.

quiz.q: Which local African fat can be used as a butterfat alternative but has a strong smell?
quiz.explanation: Shea butter is solid at room temperature but has a strong odor that needs refining.

quiz.q: What is the first sensory test for evaluating milk quality?
quiz.explanation: Smell is the quickest way to detect sour or off odors in milk.

quiz.q: What does a lactometer measure?
quiz.explanation: A lactometer measures the density of milk, indicating if it's watered down.

quiz.q: What is the normal reading for fresh milk on a lactometer at 20Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Fresh milk typically has a density of 1.026-1.032 g/ml at 20Â°C.

quiz.q: What does a clot-on-boiling test indicate?
quiz.explanation: If milk curdles when boiled, it is acidic and likely spoiled.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of good quality cream?
quiz.explanation: Good cream has a clean smell and a yellowish-white color.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pasteurization temperature and time for milk?
quiz.explanation: High-temperature short-time pasteurization is 72Â°C for 15 seconds.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using milk with high bacteria count in ice cream?
options: A) It makes ice cream too sweet
B) It can cause food poisoning
quiz.explanation: High bacteria can lead to foodborne illness and spoilage.

quiz.q: What is the typical fat content of whole milk powder?
quiz.explanation: Whole milk powder contains about 26% fat.

quiz.q: How should you store opened cans of evaporated milk?
options: B) In the refrigerator for up to 3 days
quiz.explanation: Once opened, evaporated milk should be refrigerated and used within 3 days.

quiz.q: What is a common problem when using too much whey in ice cream?
quiz.explanation: Excess whey increases lactose, which can crystallize and cause sandiness.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural emulsifier found in eggs?
quiz.explanation: Egg yolks contain lecithin, which acts as an emulsifier.

quiz.q: What is the ideal total solids content for an ice cream mix?
quiz.explanation: A good ice cream mix has 36-40% total solids for creaminess and stability.

quiz.q: Which test can be used to check the fat content of milk?
quiz.explanation: The Gerber test is a standard method for determining fat content in milk.
